newsitem.title: CHINA: China cleans up accounting to face competition.
newsitem.headline: China cleans up accounting to face competition.

text.p: China has launched a clean-up of its domestic accounting industry to raise standards and face foreign competition, officials and analysts said on Thursday.
The Ministry of Finance had recently conducted a nationwide investigation of accounting offices, punishing a number of them for irregularities, officials said.

Beijing last month also empowered the industry group, the China Association of Registered Accountants, and some government departments to overhaul the industry from August until the end of 1998, they said.
An association official said China's accounting industry, which was revived in the 1980s after the government began reforming the economy, was sorely in need of standardisation.
"Our accounting industry has lagged far behind the country's economic development," he said.
"In the latest move, we aim to enhance the professional quality and morality of accountants," he said.
"We must also keep an eye on international competition since the quality of our accountants as a whole is still far below international standards," he added.
China had allowed foreign accounting firms to set up joint ventures with Chinese partners since the early 1990s to conduct full scope audits, foreign accountants said.
Although overseas accounting firms were considered expensive, they were favoured by foreign-funded companies in China because of their high standards, they said.
Widespread irregularities, including fraud, underlined the need for change in the domestic industry, analysts said.

The Finance Ministry had found 16 percent of nearly 840,000 accounting offices checked in the past three months held false accounts of more than 14 billion yuan ($1.687 billion), the official Xinhua news agency said on Wednesday.
The ministry fined 70,000 offices, disqualified more than 200 accountants, and filed charges against 46, it said.
Major offences included keeping false accounts and fabricating information, Xinhua quoted a ministry official as saying.

In one case last year, a number of accountants conspired with Shenzhen-listed Shengli Oil Field Daming Group Co to cover up an illegal share consolidation to help the firm win the chance to issue shares to the public.
"Widespread irregularities have made many investors lose confidence in accountants," said one stock market analyst.
"Rectification is a must for China's financial markets to operate in a healthy manner and for China's accountants to compete in the international market," he said.
Officials said the current campaign would be divided into four phases.

In the first two stages, all accountants and offices at the national level would be required to conduct self-checks from August to December this year and those at regional levels from January to April next year, they said.
Beijing would conduct a large-scale probe into the results of the inspections in May and June next year, officials said.
Finally, in the second half of 1998, punitive measures would be announced and would include revoking licences if necessary, they said.
Beijing would also amend existing accounting regulations and unveil new rules, they said. Details had yet to be worked out.
China now had more than 120,000 registered accountants of whom more than 50,000 were full-time professionals, the officials said.
